newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria seeks social safety net for reforms.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria seeks social safety net for reforms.

text.p: The Bulgarian government is hoping for support from international lenders meeting in Brussels this week to alleviate the effects of a tough reform programme on its already impoverished people.

Vulnerable groups such as pensioners, the sick and the unemployed are already hard-hit by the collapse of the national currency, and a fixed exchange rate regime to be introduced in June will set more tight limits on state spending.

"To reduce the social cost of reform we will use all the reserves of the social welfare system, but for the first months after the introduction of a currency board we will have to rely on assistance from international institutions," Social Welfare Minister Ivan Neikov said in an interview.
The Group of 24 industrialised nations meet on Tuesday and Wednesday to discuss extra support for Bulgaria to accompany a standby accord agreed with the International Monetary Fund.
Bulgaria is looking to the European Union and other lenders to fill a gap of about $500 million in funding needs for the reform programme.
Under a currency board, local currency in circulation is strictly matched to central bank reserves, severely limiting the financial powers of the government.
The new parliament must approve a draft 1997 budget and legal measures to allow introduction of the currency board, which is expected in June.

A recent cabinet report said real incomes in 1996 had fallen by some 65 percent compared to their 1990 levels. "The consumption of a considerable part of the population has shrunk to around the level of biological survival," it said.
"For many people it requires a major adjustment as they have a good education and qualifications but suddenly they have found themselves living in misery," said Neikov.

He said that under a currency board, only people living below the poverty level would be eligible for state benefits, and the new government to be elected on April 19 would have to set new eligibility criteria.
For the past year or so, as Bulgaria's economic plight worsens, the welfare sector has seen its funds dry up.

Orphanages and homes for the disabled rely on donations to survive. State hospitals are forced to turn some patients away, and those who are admitted for treatment must supply their own bedsheets, medicines and food.

Unemployment hit 13.7 percent of the workforce in February and is set to rise further. Milcho Dimitrov, deputy social welfare minister and head of the National Labour Exchange, said another 160,000 workers are expected to be laid off by the end of the year, some 100,000 from industrial enterprises and around 58,000 from the public sector.
"The impact of the reform on the labour market will be eased by compensation measures by the government and crucial World Bank financial support," Dimitrov said.
The cabinet last week announced a World Bank-funded package including severance payments and grants to help some of those thrown out of work to set up small businesses.
Dimitrov said there would also be measures to encourage people to look for work and reduce welfare dependence.
The Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), which is expected to win a majority in the new parliament, expects the benefits of a currency board to be visible by December.
"As the economy stabilises, the real income of people is expected to rise two-fold by the yearend from the current levels," said senior UDF official Valentin Vassilev.
He said that macroeconomic stabilisation, and lower inflation and interest rates would improve the business environment and promote creation of new jobs.
Vassilev said a future UDF cabinet would improve tax collection, speed up privatisation and attract foreign investment to get the economy moving again.
